text:
**The Shallow End**

Everyone called him Q, and nobody could remember why. His name was Quentin Ashby-Moore, which was reason enough, but the nickname sounded earned, like a call sign. At nineteen he already seemed like a man to whom things would be entrusted.

We were roommates sophomore year. I arrived with two duffel bags and a lamp shaped like a goose. Q arrived with a mother carrying a fern and a set of sheets so crisp they seemed to give off a faint light. He shook my hand and said my name back to me, the way people are taught in seminars, except that when Q did it you felt he had been waiting to hear it. By October he knew the name of the woman who swiped our cards at the dining hall, and the names of her grandchildren, and which one had asthma.

He was not a golden boy. He was slight and a little nearsighted, and he wore the same gray sweater for weeks. He was simply good at things, all things, in a quiet, slightly apologetic way. He could fold a fitted sheet. He wrote thank-you notes to professors. When a campus officer stopped us for riding two to a bicycle down the library steps, Q asked about the photograph of a little girl clipped to his visor, and ten minutes later the officer was showing us a video of her ballet recital, and we walked the bicycle home unticketed and somehow ashamed, as if forgiven by a priest.

I loved him, the way you love people who make you feel like a rough draft. I also kept a list. It lived in the back of my geology notebook, titled "Q's Flaws," and over two years it acquired four entries:

1. Hums when he reads.
2. Says "per se" incorrectly.
3. Possibly too nice to waiters?? (Performative?)
4. Feet.

The fourth I could not defend even then. His feet were fine. I simply needed there to be a fourth thing.

Junior year, a girl I had loved for most of a semester told me at a party that she thought I was "really solid," and then asked if Q was seeing anyone. I went back to our room and lay on my bed with my shoes on. Q came in an hour later and said, without my telling him anything, "She's wrong about you, you know. 'Solid' is what you say about a table." Years later I asked him in an e-mail how he'd known, and he replied that he didn't remember the night at all, which was either the kindest or the cruelest thing he could have said.

After graduation he went to a New York firm whose name was three surnames, and I went to an Ohio newspaper that folded in my second year. We wrote for a while, then only at Christmas. Then I saw online that he had married and had a son with Q's careful, nearsighted face, and I did not write at all, because I could not think of a way to say congratulations that didn't sound like an accusation. Ten years on, I wrote copy for a dental-supply company. I was, by most measures, fine. I was solid.

My cousin got married in Baltimore in the spring, at a harbor hotel with a pool on the twelfth floor, enclosed in glass like an aquarium turned inside out. On Friday morning I woke at six, hungover from the rehearsal dinner, and decided to swim, because I had read that swimming was good for remorse.

The pool was empty. I put on my prescription goggles, tinted a faintly sinister blue, and the white silicone cap I wear because my hair is thinning. In this outfit I look, I'm told, like a thumb. I swam a bad breaststroke for twenty minutes, then stood chest-deep in the shallow end, letting the remorse settle.

That was when the door opened and Q walked in.

He was wearing a suit. He had aged in the unfair way of men who were slight at twenty: he had simply become more himself, the face sharper, the glasses better. Behind him came a woman of about thirty in a blazer and sneakers, holding two coffees. He said, "Thank you, Dana," and the exact pitch of his gratitude went into me like cold water into the ear.

He did not look at me. Why would he? I was a thumb in the shallow end. They sat at a table by the window, fifteen feet away, and the glass and tile brought every word to me with chapel-like clarity. I could have announced myself. I thought about it for almost a full second. Then I turned my back, put my elbows on the gutter, and listened.

"I wanted somewhere quiet," Q said. "To talk about the Lindqvist account. Before Hal makes the announcement."

"Okay," Dana said, and I could hear her sitting up.

"First, I want to say how much I've valued what you've brought to it. Honestly, I don't think we'd still have them without you. And I know you've been thinking about the lead role, now that Martin's leaving."

"I have," she said. "I really have."

There was a silence long enough that I heard the pool filter clear its throat.

"And what Hal and I want," Q said, "is to put you where you can really flourish. Long term. Where your particular strengths can be—centered."

"Okay," Dana said, and it had something rising in it, a hopeful lift, like a kite catching.

I knew then what was happening, the way you know a glass will fall a half second before it does. He was going to tell her she wasn't getting it. He had found a glass room at six-thirty in the morning so he could tell her gently, before Hal told her in front of everyone. It was exactly what Q would do. It had probably been planned on a legal pad. And it was going wrong.

"So the thinking," Q said, "is that the lead role is a lot of client management. A lot of travel. And we see you more as—"

"I don't mind travel," Dana said. "I know I said that thing about my sister's kids, but she has help now."

"No, of course. It's just that we see you as—the engine. Of the whole thing."

"Oh my God," Dana said. "Q. I thought you brought me up here to tell me I didn't get it."

Here was the second where he could set it right. I turned my head slightly, the goggles turning the scene a deep marine blue. Q had both hands flat on the table, the way you steady one that wobbles. I watched him decide, and I watched him fail to decide, and I watched the failure become a decision on its own.

"I—well. The thing is, it's not finalized."

"No, I know, I won't say anything until Hal does." She was laughing now, a high, wet, embarrassed laugh. "I'm sorry, I'm going to cry in a hotel pool."

"It's fine," said Q, in a voice I had never heard him use, like someone reading the wrong lines from a script.

"Thank you for fighting for me," she said. "I know you did."

She hugged him, and he hugged her back, half-rising, his tie swinging against the table. Then she went to fix her face, and the glass door hissed shut behind her, and Q was alone with me and the filter and the long blue water.

He took his glasses off, pressed the heels of his hands into his eyes, and said, quite clearly, to no one, "Oh, *fuck*."

I had waited ten years for this. Longer: since the bicycle and the ballet recital, since the sheets and the fern. I had wanted to see the seam in him, and here it was, under fluorescent light, smelling of chlorine. I had a real fourth entry now. I could have written it on my wet palm.

Instead I felt a terrible tenderness, the kind you feel for a child who has fallen in public and is trying not to cry. He would have to go downstairs and find Hal, and find Dana, and find a sentence, and there was no sentence, not even for him. He had been solid all along. Like a table. Like any of us.

He put his glasses back on. His eyes rested on me for a second, the blue goggles, the white cap, the pale thumb of my body, and there was nothing in them, only the vague courtesy of a man registering that he hadn't been alone.

"Sorry," he said across the water. "Didn't mean to disturb your swim."

I lifted one hand, the way strangers do. Then I pushed off the wall and swam, badly, toward the deep end, and I didn't come up until I heard the door.
